canberra.title: ‘The time is right’: Shorten launches pitch for UC merger with CIT
canberra.snippet: A merged Canberra Institute of Technology and University of Canberra would be able to offer more competitive and cheaper courses, as well...
canberra.content:
UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten says both organisations would be stronger if merged. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

A merged Canberra Institute of Technology and University of Canberra would be able to offer more competitive and cheaper courses, as well as stem the bleeding at the troubled vocational training organisation, UC Vice-Chancellor Bill Shorten says.

Launching his public pitch for a single post-high school education provider for Canberra, Mr Shorten said the resignation of CIT CEO Margot McNeill provided the opportunity for government and the community to consider merging the two institutions.

Mr Shorten said closer ties between UC and CIT had been on his mind since becoming Vice-Chancellor and a merger was an idea whose time had come.

“The time’s right for UC, CIT, the Canberra community and the ACT Government to talk about can we be better together: one pathway for all Canberrans post-school,” he said.

Mr Shorten said he was not reinventing the wheel, pointing to RMIT’s model in Melbourne. A merger proposal has also been on the table since 2011, following the Bradley review of the ACT Public Service, but it has not been adopted.

But CIT now had some clear air with Dr McNeill’s departure, the ACT Government was reviewing CIT governance, and it was clear that the current model was not working, racking up consecutive deficits, including $28 million in 2025.

Mr Shorten said UC was in a strong position to pursue a merger, having returned to surplus following rising enrolments.

Echoing comments made by CIT Board chair Tom Rogers, Mr Shorten said the taxpayer could not be a funding tap left on while problems were ignored.

He rejected arguments that a merger would be empire-building and would result in higher tuition costs for vocational courses, saying a single organisation would save taxpayers money, reduce duplication and create efficiencies.

“We can actually offer cheaper education as a result, because at the moment, we duplicate everything,” he said.

“If you want to go to do VET in Canberra at TAFE or you wanted to go and do uni at UC, we’ve got two separate infrastructures.

“We’re missing the boat when it comes to opportunities nationally, and we’re missing the boat when it comes to opportunities internationally.

“Rather than it duplicating two back offices, let’s work together to grow the pie and then free up resources for teaching, free up resources for research, free up resources for industry engagement.”

Federal Education Minister Jason Clare says the artificial barrier between TAFE and university needs to be broken down. Photo: Jason Clare Facebook.

Mr Shorten said a merger would also free up land, such as the CIT Bruce campus, for other uses and add to that pie.

He said UC and CIT had already created degree pathways for vocational students, and that a merger would accelerate the breakdown of study barriers between the two organisations, providing more choice and access.

This was important in the era of artificial intelligence.

“With the rise of AI, we can’t afford necessarily just to rely on systems which have been around for 50 years, and in fact we need to see if we can we do things better, and create together a brighter future,” Mr Shorten said.

It would also open the way for a “long overdue” UC presence on the southside, in Greenway, for example.

Mr Shorten said he saw no reason why CIT could not retain its own identity and brand within a unified entity.

Next steps included making a submission to the governance review, discussing the idea with Mr Rogers and engaging with staff, industry and the Canberra community.

ACT Skills, Training and Industrial Relations Minister Michael Pettersson said the government was open to a range of governance improvements or alternative models that may arise from its review.

“Any proposal for more significant structural change or mergers with other institutions would need to demonstrate clear benefits for students and the ACT, secure broad support from both institutions, and be subject to thorough consultation with staff and stakeholders,” he said.

“There is merit in continuing to explore opportunities for closer collaboration where they can deliver better outcomes for students.”

Last month, Mr Pettersson invited stakeholders, including UC and other Canberra-based universities, to participate in the review.

The conversation had only begun, but Mr Shorten was heartened by the support he had received, particularly from Federal Education Minister Jason Clare.

Mr Clare said it was an idea that should be explored.

“We need to break down the artificial barrier between TAFE and university,” he said.

“Closer collaboration could make it easier for students to get the qualifications they need and help build the workforce Canberra needs.”

Member for Bean David Smith said a merger would give CIT the reset it needed and the opportunity for a stronger higher education presence in southern Canberra.

“UC should think not just about a combined presence in the Woden Valley, but in the Tuggeranong Valley as well,” he said.

“The future of our community depends on the skills, knowledge and adaptability of its people. I believe this merger will help in securing that future.”

ACT Senators Katy Gallagher and David Pocock also came out in support of a merger.

National Tertiary Education Union ACT secretary Lachlan Clohesy said a single front door to tertiary education in the ACT would be an excellent outcome for students.

Mr Clohesy said credit transfers and recognition of prior learning were much easier to navigate within a single organisation rather than going between two educational institutions.

He said dual-sector universities such as RMIT, Victoria University and Swinburne University in Victoria worked well.

“It is not a new idea and may well be the best way forward for Canberra’s students,” Mr Clohesy said.

He said the idea of bringing UC and CIT together was consistent with the Federal Government’s aims.

But Mr Clohesy said the numbers needed to stack up to avoid negative outcomes for staff, and governance arrangements had to be fit for purpose.

Others were more cautious.

Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton said a merger could be the way forward, but the party was examining all options for CIT.

ACT Greens education spokesperson Laura Nuttall said the party was open to the proposal if staff and students of both UC and CIT were fully consulted and supportive.

“We note that a merged vocational education institution and university has worked as a model in Victoria through RMIT, but we will await full detail on what a merger might look like before taking a stance on whether it is the right model in this case,” she said.

CPSU Regional Secretary Maddy Northam said members at CIT needed stability not more change.

“CPSU members at CIT are fatigued by all this change,” she said. “They have seen change in leadership now talk of further change. All this while they are facing a round of job cuts.

“Members are concerned about the impact on CIT service delivery, students and their jobs. They have more questions than answers.”

canberra.title: Bystanders intervene after woman allegedly assaults two staff members at mall
canberra.snippet: Two retail store workers were allegedly assaulted by the same woman at Westfield Belconnen before bystanders intervened. An ACT Policing ...
canberra.content:
A 37-year-old woman is accused of committing several offences at Westfield Belconnen. Photo: Westfield Belconnen.

Two retail store workers were allegedly assaulted by the same woman at Westfield Belconnen before bystanders intervened.

An ACT Policing spokesperson alleged the 37-year-old from Spence had gone to a department store and became involved in an altercation with staff around midday on Wednesday (12 August).

She allegedly approached a staff member and repeatedly shouted at her before assaulting her, then damaged several items in the store.

It is alleged the woman then assaulted a second staff member before members of the public intervened.

“Police and security responded to the incident and located the woman inside the store,” the police spokesperson said.

“She was subsequently arrested and conveyed to the ACT Watch House.”

The woman was charged with two counts of common assault as well as single counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm, property damage and affray.

When she briefly faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Thursday (13 August), both the prosecutor and her defence lawyer asked for her to be taken to hospital for a mental health assessment.

Chief Magistrate Louise Taylor ordered that she be taken for such an assessment and then return to court in the future. The woman will not be named while the assessment takes place.

The police spokesperson said anyone who saw the incident can contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or via the website. Quote reference number 8469520.

canberra.title: ATO paid $12 million to ‘virtual’ Griffith winery that told it turnover was under $2 million
canberra.snippet: The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) paid more than $12 million in GST refunds to a small Griffith winery over 14 months, despite the bus...
canberra.content:
Sans Pareil Estate was a small winery located in Hanwood that received millions in GST refunds from the tax office. Photo: Supplied.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) paid more than $12 million in GST refunds to a small Griffith winery over 14 months, despite the business telling the ATO when it registered for GST that its expected annual turnover was less than $2 million, an exclusive Region investigation has found.

Court documents have revealed the ATO made 15 GST refund payments to Hanwood-based Sans Pareil Estate between April 2021 and June 2022. The largest single payment was $2.5 million.

On one occasion, the ATO paid Sans Pareil $1.73 million based on an invoice for more than $19 million worth of wine. The supplier later told the ATO it had never issued that invoice for that amount, which also contained an incorrect Australian Business Number (ABN).

Region asked the ATO whether it generally checked if ABNs were correct before making million-dollar GST refund payments.

The ATO did not answer the question.

Aaron Salvestrin, 31, launched Sans Pareil Estate from a shed in Hanwood in 2018 and remained its owner and director until the company collapsed into liquidation four years later, with an alleged debt to the ATO of more than $30 million. For most of its operation, the wine business had less than five employees.

Earlier this year, Mr Salvestrin pleaded guilty to three fraud offences after admitting his business altered supplier invoices to claim millions of dollars in GST refunds from the ATO to which it was not entitled.

He is due to be sentenced in the NSW District Court in November.

How the GST refunds were claimed

According to a statement of facts tendered in court, Mr Salvestrin registered Sans Pareil as an export business and told the ATO it was selling large quantities of wine to a European buyer.

Rather than producing its own wine, Sans Pareil bought bulk wine from other wineries and marketed it under its own brand.

Businesses generally do not charge GST on goods exported overseas, meaning Sans Pareil could claim back GST it had supposedly paid when purchasing bulk wine from Australian suppliers for export.

Court documents state that in an interview with the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Mr Salvestrin described Sans Pareil as a “virtual winery” and said his role was as the “jack of all trades”.

He admitted his company used PDF software to alter genuine invoices issued by wine suppliers and inflate the figures on them so it could claim GST refunds to which it was not entitled.

Aaron Salvestrin was once touted as a rising star of the industry. Photo: Sans Pareil.

The $19 million invoice

When Sans Pareil applied for GST registration, it told the ATO its expected business turnover was between $150,000 and $1,999,999.

Yet, according to court documents, it later submitted a single invoice to the ATO for just over $19 million worth of wine allegedly purchased from Kingston Estate Pty Ltd.

The ATO promptly paid Sans Pareil a GST refund of more than $1.73 million.

During a later audit of Sans Pareil, the South Australian winery told the ATO it had never issued the invoice.

It also said the document contained an incorrect ABN and that the entity named on the invoice did not even sell bulk wine.

More multi-million dollar invoices

The statement of facts revealed Sans Pareil also submitted 10 invoices to the ATO purportedly from Victorian-based Andrew Peace Wines, for bulk wine purchases ranging from $5 million to $24 million. The invoices claimed more than $105 million in purchases.

The ATO paid GST refunds on most of those invoices.

During the later audit, Andrew Peace Wines also told the ATO it had not issued any of them.

The ATO finally initiated the audit of Sans Pareil in June 2022, asking the company to provide documents proving its five largest tax invoices filed in May 2022 were genuine.

“I am very nervous,” Mr Salvestrin told an associate while the audit was ongoing in August 2022, according to the statement of facts.

The associate later told auditors: “The export business was non-existent and no wine left the country”.

In an interview with the AFP, Mr Salvestrin admitted many of the invoices he submitted to the ATO were false.

He also admitted directing an employee, identified in the statement of facts as “BP”, to enter incorrect sales data into Xero.

Mr Salvestrin said BP was completely unaware of the fraud and that he “felt bad” about involving the employee.

During the audit process, the ATO rejected three claims for GST refunds between August and October 2022, shortly before the company went into liquidation.

Audit and liquidation

The ATO audit concluded Sans Pareil fabricated tax invoices to claim GST refunds.

Court documents state that while Mr Salvestrin claimed the GST refunds went back into his business, the audit found a number of purchases were considered “personal” and not business related. This included $31,000 for private jet service Navair and $101,000 for a universal home theatre system.

In total, Sans Pareil made $17 million worth of GST refund claims.

It owes the ATO just over $30 million, including interest and penalties.

Liquidator documents listed 21 vehicles owned by the wine company, including a rare McLaren P1 which had a door sill signed by F1 star Daniel Ricciardo. It was sold for $1.47 million.

An annual update report provided by the liquidator in December 2025 revealed that just $2.8 million of the more than $30 million owed had been recovered in just over three years since the company’s collapse.

A McLaren P1 sold for $1.47 million as part of the liquidation of Sans Pareil. The vehicle had a door sill signed by F1 star Daniel Ricciardo. Photo: Road and Track.

What did the ATO know?

Region asked the ATO what checks, if any, it carried out on the invoices submitted by Sans Pareil before approving the refunds.

We also asked whether it had recovered any of the more than $30 million owed and whether it expected to recover the money.

“The ATO is unable to comment on specific cases due to our obligations under taxpayer confidentiality laws,” a spokesperson said.

Region also asked how common it was for businesses reporting turnover below $2 million to receive GST refunds of more than $1 million.

The ATO did not respond.

The ATO also declined to answer questions about what safeguards it had to identify businesses claiming unusually large GST refunds compared with their reported turnover, and whether it had changed its GST refund processes as a result of the Sans Pareil case or other similar cases.

An ATO spokesperson provided the following general comments.

“Australia’s tax system relies on self-assessment, with every taxpayer responsible for lodging correct returns – and most taxpayers do the right thing. The system is designed to make it easy for legitimate businesses to access GST refunds without unnecessary delays. Unfortunately, a small minority of taxpayers seek to exploit the system, and the ATO has sophisticated tools and intelligence capabilities to detect and address this behaviour,” the spokesperson said.

“The ATO takes attempts to defraud the GST system seriously and works to both recover revenue and prevent asset dissipation. GST fraud is not a victimless crime. It diverts funds that would otherwise support essential services such as healthcare, infrastructure, and education.

“We continually strengthen and refine our risk detection capabilities in response to changing behaviours and emerging risks, helping ensure taxpayers pay the right amount of tax in accordance with the law.

“We use all the tools at our disposal to recoup fraudulently obtained funds. This can include issuing director penalty notices, garnishee bank accounts, issuing departure prohibition orders and prosecution actions, as well as working with the AFP on proceeds of crime actions.”

If you know more about this story, contact Oliver on 0498 843 181, or by email: ojacques@region.com.au

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Social media content creator allegedly chokes brother unconscious, assaults father
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence. A social media content creator has been accused of choking his brother u...
canberra.content:
13 August 2026

A 23-year-old social media content creator has been granted bail on family violence charges. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This article refers to alleged family violence.

A social media content creator has been accused of choking his brother unconscious and assaulting their father when he tried to intervene.

The 23-year-old, who hasn’t been named to avoid identifying his two family members, has almost 150,000 followers on his Instagram page and nearly 25,000 on TikTok. He posts athletic and exercise content.

The ACT Magistrates Court heard how on Wednesday (12 August), he was alleged to have choked and assaulted his brother, then also assaulted their father.

He was arrested and handed two counts of assault and one of choking before applying for bail on Thursday (13 August), which was opposed on the risk of him endangering the safety or welfare of others.

Prosecutor Sophia Newton said the allegations demonstrated a “persistent and violent act of family violence”.

She said the man was alleged to have choked his brother unconscious, even though he was only unconscious briefly. He allegedly continued the attack despite the intervention of their father.

Ms Newton argued that the man’s alleged actions were disproportionate to any provocation from his brother.

“Well, on your case, the defendant has provided an explanation for why he did what he did,” Chief Magistrate Louise Taylor said.

The man’s defence lawyer, from Legal Aid, said he had lived with his brother and father for some time, although occasionally stayed with his partner.

She said he had no prior criminal history and could live with his partner if granted bail.

Chief Magistrate Taylor said there was no suggestion either his brother or father had been subjected to violence before and granted bail on conditions including he not contact nor approach them and live at his partner’s home in southern Canberra.

She said if he saw either of his family members on the street, “the obligation is on him to turn his back and walk away”.

Also, the chief magistrate warned him that any messaging or posting on social media that could be construed to be a message to his brother or father could be seen to be a breach of his bail.

The matter was adjourned to September. No pleas were entered.

If this story has raised any concerns for you, 1800RESPECT, the national 24-hour sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line, can be contacted on 1800 737 732. Help and support are also available through the Domestic Violence Crisis Service ACT on 02 6280 0900 and Lifeline on 13 11 14. In an emergency, call triple zero.

australia.title: ‘Melancholic fantasy’: Wong escalates Labor rhetoric against Hanson, condemning ‘monoculture’ comment
australia.snippet: Foreign affairs minister and first Asian-Australian to serve in federal cabinet to use Lowy Institute address to criticise politicians st...
australia.content:
Labor has escalated its pushback on One Nation’s surging political support, with the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, labelling Pauline Hanson’s push for a monoculture a “melancholic fantasy” that would harm national security.

Wong, the first Asian-Australian to serve in federal cabinet, will use a major address at The Lowy Institute on Friday to criticise politicians stoking racial divisions, insisting the country’s multicultural success remains a national asset.

“The call for a monoculture is a call for Australia to curtail our choices and cut off our connections,” Wong will say, according to a preview of the speech.

“To look inwards, to have no friends to work with, no partners to trade with, no opportunities to grow from. To be lonely in a dangerous world.”

Hanson said in June that Australia must exist as a “monocultural society”, blaming high levels of overseas migration for a loss of national identity and values. In a speech criticised across the political spectrum, the One Nation leader conceded modern Australia was multiracial, adding that only one “cultural umbrella” should exist.

In one of the strongest rebuttals yet from Labor, Wong argues Hanson risks damaging the national interest and badly undermining social cohesion.

“But well before we could ever realise this melancholic fantasy of monoculture, there is a lot of damage that can be done,” she will say.

“Because Australians would be turned against each other. Australia would be a more hostile place. Harder to be family, harder to be a friend, colleague or neighbour.”

Warning forces within the country and overseas are seeking to divide Australians, Wong warns against politicians seeking to pit different sections of the community against others.

“Turning Australians against each other is the opposite of patriotism. Our resilience starts with how we choose to live together.”

Wong’s intervention comes as record support for One Nation reshapes the political landscape. In last month’s Guardian Essential poll the party attracted 25% of the primary vote, behind Labor on 31% but ahead of the Coalition’s 22%.

Her address – in an annual lecture named for diplomat and intelligence boss Allan Gyngell – includes a re-ordering of Australia’s foreign policy priorities to put the Indo-Pacific region first.

In response to a speech by Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, in January, in which he lamented the decline of the post second world war, rules-based order and called for middle powers to act together more strategically, Wong says Australia has been at work on the task since Labor’s 2022 election victory.

She points to multilateral organisations including the Pacific Islands Forum and enhanced cooperation with the European Union, as well as closer cooperation with Quad partners as evidence.

But Wong says resilience should be a key focus for the Albanese government.

“Nations face weaponised supply chains, flagrant disinformation, and foreign interference that seeks to weaken us from within, as well as the challenges posed by artificial intelligence.

“AI alone is an era-defining technology – reshaping economies, societies and national power – with benefits and risks in every domain. It is connecting the globe, and dividing it.

“It will spread faster and disrupt more than any revolutionary technology before it.”

australia.title: ‘Lauf’ and ‘minceur’: the words that made a 13-year-old from Melbourne a world Scrabble champion
australia.snippet: Dineth Fernando – who moved to Australia with his family in February – says he just needed to ‘find the word and play – that’s all’ Get o...
australia.content:
Dineth Fernando’s first language isn’t English and he only arrived in Melbourne six months ago – but already he’s claimed an international Scrabble title with an Australian flag draped around his shoulders.

The 13-year-old won the 2026 world youth Scrabble championships in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi over the weekend, becoming the third Australian representative in the competition’s history to take out the prize.

During the three-day tournament, Dineth played 24 games of the classic word game, going head-to-head against more than 130 opponents from 15 different countries.

“It took a lot of stress and effort to navigate through the days,” Dineth, who moved with his family in February from Sri Lanka, said.

“But I just needed to concentrate on the game, nothing else.

“Like, don’t care if there is a live camera going on, I just needed to jumble the rack, find the word and play – that’s all.”

This was Dineth’s third attempt at the world championships, and the trip to Nairobi had already forced him to contend with jetlag on top of the nerves.

But after more than 20 hours of play, and carefully placed words including “lauf” (a run in bobsleighing), “novelese” (a style of writing characteristic of poor novels), “minceur” (a French word for thinness), “histrio” (an archaic word meaning actor) and “postering”, the 13-year-old emerged victorious on Sunday.

Prasanna Fernando almost cried when his son was crowned the world youth Scrabble champion.

“It feels unreal,” Fernando said.

“I sometimes still can’t believe he actually won it because the level of competition was extremely high.

“But I always knew he was capable of doing it one day.”

Dineth got his first taste for the game when he and his family were still living in Sri Lanka.

At eight years old, he joined the school Scrabble club before hiring a private coach as he flew all over the country to compete.

His family moved to Australia in February for his father’s work, but he continued his pursuit for Scrabble greatness, entering competitions and playing against people like Melbourne-based two-time Scrabble world champion and 2006 youth Scrabble winner David Eldar, and even beating world champion finalist Harshan Lamabadusuriya.

His accolades quickly grew, becoming runner-up at the Wodonga open Scrabble championship, winning the Ballarat open championship and eventually taking out the Australian youth prize.

Scrabble Victoria secretary, Carol Johnsen, has faced the teenager a few times, and though he had luck on his side, she says he is also a force to be reckoned with.

“He is an astounding player,” she said.

“The tiles just flowed for him: he got the X and the Z and the Q and they all went in the right places.

“I had no hope, and he’s beat me by over 200 points each time.”

Dineth spends more than three hours a day studying Scrabble words and believes his discipline and hard work gave him an edge at the youth competition.

Though English is not his first language, he does not see this as an issue, since the game’s dictionary is a combination of many languages including English, Latin, French and more.

Nigel Richards, a five-time world champion became famous for winning Scrabble tournaments in languages he didn’t speak, taking out the French title in 2015 and 2018, and the Spanish-language competition in 2024.

For those at the top levels of Scrabble, it is closer to mathematics and pattern recognition than a language game, according to Johnsen.

But Dineth’s favourite thing about Scrabble is the opportunity it offers for him to learn new words.

After an almost 12,000km trip home, the 13-year-old returned to school on Thursday, where a hero’s welcome was waiting.

“It was a really great feeling that everyone – my friends and teachers – wished me,” he said.

He’s now got his eyes on the 2027 competition and is hoping to become the first youth champion to defend their title.

australia.title: Former Catholic bishop accused of hosting alcohol-fuelled parties to sexually abuse Aboriginal men found guilty
australia.snippet: Christopher Alan Saunders found guilty of 13 sex offences in West Australian district court on Thursday. He was acquitted of six other ch...
australia.content:
A former high-ranking Catholic known for hosting boozy shirts-off parties has been convicted of sexually abusing two young Aboriginal men.

Former bishop of Broome Christopher Alan Saunders, 76, was found guilty of 13 sex offences on Thursday following a jury trial in the West Australian district court.

The offending between 2008 and 2019 included one count of sexual penetration without consent and a dozen unlawful and indecent assault charges.

He was acquitted of six other charges, including two counts of indecently dealing with a child over 16 under his authority and four counts of unlawful and indecent assault.

Saunders was ordained as the second Broome bishop in 1996 and presided over 13 schools and nine parishes, before stepping aside in 2020 when the sex abuse claims became public.

Pope Francis accepted his resignation a year later.

Unless acquitted on appeal, Saunders would be the highest-ranking Catholic in Australia convicted of sexual abuse while a member of the clergy.

The late cardinal George Pell was found guilty in 2018 but later acquitted by the high court of raping one choirboy and molesting another in 1996.

Prosecutors said Saunders, known as Brother B by his victims, put on alcohol-fuelled parties at Catholic church-owned properties to get access to Aboriginal boys and men so he could sexually assault them.

“The accused had a sexual interest in young Aboriginal men and a tendency to act on that interest when the opportunity presented itself,” the prosecutor, Adam Ebell, said.

Saunders, who studied law before becoming the first diocesan priest ordained in WA’s Kimberley region in 1976, exploited the power imbalance between himself and the younger men, Ebell said.

The main complainant, who cannot be named for legal reasons, said he was 16 when the then bishop started grooming him at a Broome home in regular visits during which he was given alcohol.

The interactions over the decade that followed involved kissing, naked wrestling, touching of private areas and penetrative sex, he said.

Saunders denied the sexual assaults took place.

His lawyer Tony Hager said the three complainants, were convicted criminals with long records who had abused alcohol and drugs during their lives which affected their memories.

Saunders was acquitted of a further seven charges mid-trial due to insufficient evidence being presented to the jury.

australia.title: Pentagon official and former Aukus sceptic says deal is ‘full steam ahead’, echoing Trump
australia.snippet: Elbridge Colby, a US under secretary of war, says he is ‘very pleased’ with the nuclear submarine program’s progress Get our breaking new...
australia.content:
Elbridge Colby, the third-highest-ranking official at the Pentagon and formerly an avowed Aukus sceptic, has mirrored his president’s language on the nuclear submarine deal, saying it is “full steam ahead”.

Colby, a US under secretary of war, was the author of the Trump administration’s review of the Aukus deal, which would see the US sell three in-service Virginia-class submarines to Australia, before the development of Australia’s domestically built Aukus-class submarines.

The original draft of Colby’s review was understood to be sceptical about the Aukus agreement’s prospects of success, but was rewritten – on some accounts twice – to more closely align with the president’s position that Aukus was “full steam ahead”.

Colby told an Asia-Pacific press briefing on Thursday “we’re very pleased to say that Aukus is – as the president said – full steam ahead”.

He said the Pentagon was “very pleased with the progress that has been made since the conclusion of the Aukus review which … has provided a roadmap for the success of the Aukus program.

“We all know this is an historic endeavour on the part of both countries, but particularly for Australia.”

The first Virginia-class submarine is slated to be sold to Australia in 2032.

“We remain optimistic but also clear-eyed about what we all need to do,” Colby said. “We will just keep knocking down the targets on our side. We have every expectation the Australian side will do the same.”

He said the US had “no better ally” than Australia, and that the US and Australia enjoyed a “deep alignment of thinking”.

“Australia really sees things through the lens of collective defence and a strategy of deterrence by denial designed to sustain a balance of power in this key region.”

Colby was asked about production rates of Virginia-class submarines, and also the potential presence of nuclear-armed submarines at Australian ports.

US boat-building rates have remained stubbornly laggard. It is currently manufacturing Virginia-class submarines at a rate of 1.1 to 1.2 a year.

That rate needs to be lifted to two boats a year to service US needs alone, and 2.33 boats a year in order to sell any to Australia.

Colby said the Pentagon was “very focused on submarine production, submarine maintenance, and making sure that that’s in as strong a place as it can be”.

He said the Pentagon and broader Trump administration had “a very clear understanding” with Australia about its expectations under the Aukus agreement.

“They know what is required, we’ve been very clear in private with them.

“[Those discussions were] designed to give everybody a reasonable, stable and realistic set of expectations to achieve this historic ambition that will put us all in a stronger place.”

Colby did not comment on the potential of nuclear-armed US submarines docking at Australian ports.

The US maintains a policy of “strategic ambiguity” around its nuclear capabilities, refusing to confirm or deny whether its nuclear-capable platforms – including aircraft submarines – are carrying nuclear warheads.

The Australian Department of Defence says it respects the US policy and does not ask whether platforms – such as B-52 bombers landing on Australian soil – are nuclear-armed.

Colby’s comments came in the same week an inquiry into Aukus held public hearings in Sydney, Newcastle and Port Kembla.

The former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull told the inquiry Australia’s blind faith in the Aukus submarine deal was “stark staring bonkers”, and argued the asymmetric deal with the US would likely result in no submarines at all for Australia.

Giving evidence to the inquiry in Sydney, Turnbull said the US was prevented by its own legislation from selling any submarines to Australia if that would “degrade” its own fleet.

australia.title: Reformers associate may have ‘boasted’ or ‘lied’ about a $15,000 commitment from Angus Taylor, Icac hears
australia.snippet: Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney denies ever asking federal opposition leader for money for Liberal power brokers Fo...
australia.content:
A factional ally of Angus Taylor has denied ever asking the federal opposition leader for money for a group of Liberal party Christian power brokers who allegedly solicited illegal donations, suggesting a Reformers associate may have “lied” about a $15,000 commitment.

The Catholic Schools NSW chief executive, Dallas McInerney, gave evidence at the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Thursday. Icac is investigating whether McInerney arranged and approved donations from the governing body for 600 Catholic schools to support alleged branch stacking efforts of the conservative Christian group the Reformers.

On Thursday, McInerney was asked about a message to Reformer Robert Assaf in March 2021.

In the message, which Assaf shared with other members of the group, McInerney said he had a “breakfast club with ministers”, asking for an update on “SCD [state council delegate] progress in the last six to 12 months”.

“I want to shake down Angus for 10k,” McInerney wrote. On Thursday, McInerney said the message referred to a breakfast meeting with NSW Liberal ministers, as well as a separate request to Taylor, but said the money would have been for “support for upcoming internal elections” and not the Reformers.

He said any money would have gone to “printing brochures, pamphlets, postage, mailout”.

McInerney was asked about a subsequent message sent by Reformers associate Dylan Whitelaw to members of the group days later, in which he wrote: “Dallas has told me he got the commitment from Angus, the 15k injection plus a 3k monthly donation!”

He said: “The only explanation I can venture, noting this is not my exchange of correspondence, is that I did emerge from that meeting [with Taylor] with an in-principle support … [for] the internal elections for the conservative faction.”

Pressed by counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, on why Whitelaw might have thought the money was for the Reformers, he said that one of “a number of explanations” was that Whitelaw had lied. “He lied … He boasted. He lied,” suggested McInerney.

When asked about the messages at the inquiry last month, Whitelaw said he did not recall sending them, nor did he recall Taylor making a financial contribution to the Reformers.

McInerney, who said he had never asked Taylor for money for the Reformers, said he could not recall if Taylor made a commitment of $15,000, or an ongoing commitment of $3,000 for internal elections.

The only senior Liberal he could recall having contributed directly to the Reformers was the late former federal vice-president, Teena McQueen, who died in June.

Taylor has not been named in Icac’s allegations and has repeatedly denied he ever made payments to the Reformers. On Thursday he reiterated to a press conference that he would not provide a running commentary on Icac’s hearings.

One of Taylor’s staffers, Kane Silom, was criticised after he rebuked Network Ten journalist Ashleigh Raper for asking Taylor whether he had spoken with McInerney about sending money to the Reformers.

After the press conference ended, with cameras still running, Silom said to Raper: “Are your ratings that bad? Seriously, that’s a fricking disgrace.”

The inquiry has heard the Reformers wanted more conservative policies on issues such as same-sex marriage, abortion and euthanasia. A document drafted around the group’s inception proposed to recruit 5,000 Christian conservatives to join New South Wales Liberal party branches “and thereby take control of the NSW division of the Liberal party”.

‘Spectacularly unsuccessful in their ambitions’

McInerney also told the inquiry he sought advice from then-New South Wales treasurer, Dominic Perrottet, about two key Reformers, whose company was engaged by Catholic Schools NSW without tender to provide “public relations and government services”.

Catholic Schools NSW became the first client of Beckington, a company run by Christian Ellis, and Jeremy Greenwood. The two conservative catholic Liberal operatives were paid a $10,000 retainer and $6,000 a month – $130,900 in total between August 2019 and August 2021, Icac has heard.

Greenwood’s company, JPG Advisory, was paid $135,000 between December 2021 and December 2023.

McInerney agreed he did not consider any other lobbyists before awarding the contract to Beckington.

The inquiry is looking at whether the Reformers issued sham invoices to various groups, including Catholic Schools NSW, to disguise the donations.

McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he previously said in a statement.

McInerney on Thursday admitted he first became aware of Reformers’ recruitment events in late 2018 and 2019. He said he was “mostly” supportive of their goals.

Curtin asked: “What’s the qualification here, Mr McInerney?”

“They were spectacularly unsuccessful in their ambitions,” he replied. “I never thought the model was right.”

McInerney on Thursday accepted he had begun to speak frequently to Reformers Ellis, Robert Assaf and Jean-Claude Perrottet by 2020. Asked if he knew that the men were “fervent” in the pursuit of the Reformers’ goals, McInerney said the word was “very subjective”.

Asked if “passionate” was a better word, he said: “I actually don’t think there was a passion there. I think it was a calling for them, a duty.”

Nearly 80% of funding managed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from federal and state sources, or about $3.8bn in 2024.

On Thursday, Icac produced a WhatsApp from Ellis in 2020 saying that the Reformers were targeting “like minded conservatives”, who could “dip into their government relations budget to help fund our cause.”

McInerney was grilled about emails in which he provided detailed advice to Ellis about drawing up the pitch for Catholic Schools.

“You’re telling him to get an ABN and a mail box. You are telling Mr Ellis how he can pitch to Catholic Schools NSW,” Curtin said.

“I was letting him know what were our needs and requirements,” McInerney said. “This is a traditional due diligence.”

“I want to suggest to Mr McInerney that it is anything but due diligence. You are a lawyer by training, Mr McInerney … you’re telling him that he should put in content about how to help build communication channels. That suggests that he was not the right person for the job,” Curtin said.

McInerney said it was an “iterative process” and denied he was attempting to provide “a veneer of legitimacy” to the contract.

McInerney said he sought advice from Dominic Perrottet about Ellis and Greenwood and “their parliamentary experience”.

“I can’t remember what he said. It was favourable, he knew both the individuals,” McInerney said.

McInerney said he did not talk to Damien Tudehope, Ellis’s employer until July 2020. Ellis had been asked to leave the minister’s office.

On Thursday, the inquiry heard that McInerney, the only CEO of Catholic Schools NSW since its founding in 2017, joined the Liberal party while at school in the late 1980s or early 1990s. He remained a member until June this year, when he also ceased being the president of the Mittagong branch.

McInerney admitted to having his own political ambitions “off and on for several” years, but said he was “at peace” with not taking over the late federal Liberal senator Jim Molan’s seat. Molan died in January 2023 but McInerney missed out on the Senate spot.

He was read messages exchanged between him and Greenwood in which he wrote: “I know I’ve been fucked.”

After evidence on Wednesday, the NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, removed upper house member Chris Rath as her representative on the Liberal party’s state executive. The commission heard evidence that Rath helped Reformers avoid summons for a 2023 parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe.

The shadow planning and arts minister, who received a caution from the parliamentary privileges committee in 2023 and recused himself from the parliamentary inquiry, has been referred to the privileges committee a second time over the incident. He has not been named as a person of interest in Icac’s allegations, and remains on the front bench.

Icac’s inquiry continues.

– additional reporting by Krishani Dhanji

world.title: Zambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rival
world.snippet: Hakainde Hichilema is bidding for second term, but feud between him and family of Edgar Lungu, who died in 2025, continues As Zambians go...
world.content:
As Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections.

Hakainde Hichilema, 64, is bidding for a second term leading the southern African country after defeating his arch-rival Edgar Lungu by a landslide in 2021.

A feud between the two men, their families and supporters has dominated Zambian politics, to the extent that the quarrel has continued even after Lungu died in South Africa in June 2025.

Zambia’s government went to court to try to stop the burial of Lungu by his family, who did not want Hichilema presiding over a state funeral. In June, South Africa’s supreme court of appeal ruled in favour of Lungu’s family, overturning a previous high court decision in favour of the government.

In this election, Hichilema is facing the Tonse Alliance of opposition parties led by Brian Mundubile, 55, who was a government chief whip under Lungu. Mundubile’s running mate Makebi Zulu acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson during the burial row, and on the campaign trail the two men have promised to bring Lungu’s body back to Zambia for a dignified burial.

The way death is dealt with is very important in Zambia, said Christopher Vandome, a senior research fellow at the thinktank Chatham House. “Even Hichilema supporters want to see due respect given to those that have died,” he said. “When it appears things get messy, it just makes the incumbent look disrespectful.”

The shadow of Lungu has also hung over allegations by the Tonse Alliance that Hichilema has deployed authoritarian tactics during the election campaign, including raiding its offices and detaining 36 members of Mundubile’s team.

Hichilema’s team furiously denied the claims, invoking Lungu’s treatment of Hichilema during the last election. “Zambians know what repression looks like. In 2021, the opposition leader [Hichilema] had been arrested 15 times, Prime TV [a private station] and the Post [a newspaper] had been shut down, and on election day the internet was switched off,” said a spokesperson for the ruling United Party for National Development. “Today the opposition campaigns freely across all 10 provinces, no media house has been closed and the airwaves are open.”

Transparency International Zambia monitors have recorded incidents of police interrupting opposition rallies, said Tamika Halwiindi, a coordinator at the organisation. “Disruptions from the police citing issues to do with safety have been noted to be more biased against the opposition and independents, as opposed to … the ruling party,” she said.

During Hichilema’s term, activists have also reported having peaceful demonstrations shut down. Mputa Ngalande of the Fight Inequality Alliance said he was among a group detained for more than 12 hours in July 2024 when they were protesting against the state power company during a period of 22-hour-a-day blackouts.

Vandome said: “[Hichilema’s] prospects of winning are very high. But his … personal lived experience of how complicated Zambian elections can be has given him this insecurity which is actually counting against him … denting his image in a way he doesn’t have to.”

Zambia’s economy has stabilised since an economic crisis, which was triggered when it defaulted on its debts in 2020 under Lungu. Annual inflation is now 6.5%, compared with 24.6% in July 2021. The government made primary and secondary education free in 2022.

Meanwhile, Zambia has attracted more international investment in recent years due to its huge deposits of copper, a key material in green technologies.

At the start of the month, in a giveaway to young voters, Hichilema, also known by his initials HH and nickname Bally (a slang word for an elder), told a crowd of jubilant university students that he was increasing their accommodation allowance by 50% with immediate effect.

However, the cost of living could still count against Hichilema in the elections, in which almost 8.8 million registered voters will also choose MPs and local councillors. The average annual income rose from $1,127 to $1,318 between 2021 and 2025, according to World Bank data. But prices almost doubled over the same period.

“What people are asking is: ‘If we are doing well economically, why are we not feeling impact on the ground?’” said Ngalende. “Because you will find on the ground that it is very difficult to access three meals a day.”

world.title: At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe
world.snippet: Operation under way to rescue dozens missing after boat overturned by waves at world’s largest human-made lake At least 44 people have di...
world.content:
At least 44 people have died after an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, police said.

The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales.

A crew member told the national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passenger told ZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps.

A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing.

Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon in posts on X twice in the space of 32 minutes. In the first post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.

A video shared by ZBC on Tuesday showed several people appearing to be sitting on the upturned ferry, while at least four speedboats came to their aid and a helicopter circled overhead.

Maxwell Kanhema Page, who describes himself as a media practitioner and originally posted the video shared by ZBC, reshared a video on his Facebook page filmed from the shore, in which he had noted that the lake was “angry”.

He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity.

It is not uncommon for boats to overturn on the lake. In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five drowned in a 2021 incident and three were feared dead in an October 2023 capsizing. The month before, a police boat overturned although no one died.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report.

world.title: Halting the march of the African armyworm: a natural cure offers hope to farmers
world.snippet: South African scientist’s breakthrough research shows soil fungus could be used in fight against devastating crop pest Hearing about fiel...
world.content:
Hearing about fields full of dead caterpillars enveloped in a mysterious white substance intrigued the South African scientist Letodi Luki Mathulwe. Something was killing off the African armyworm – one of the most devastating pests for farmers in east and southern Africa.

The white substance was a naturally occurring fungus and it was wiping out the caterpillar, which gained its name from its march-like advance through fields of crops.

An outbreak of African armyworm (Spodoptera exempta) in 2025 had started in northern South Africa and by April had reached the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal, where Mathulwe was working for the agriculture department. Every day she was getting panicked calls from local farmers who were finding the caterpillars in their fields.

Mathulwe went out to the KwaZulu-Natal countryside to see for herself and it was there, in the fields of Kikuyu grass – crucial grazing for livestock – that she realised she had made an important discovery.

“Something was killing the insects naturally. I was intrigued because in other areas the insects were alive and destroying the grass but as soon as they come here, there’s something that is killing them,” she said.

As an entomologist who had studied the use of fungi to kill insect pests, Mathulwe immediately gathered samples of the dead armyworms and the fungus to test at her laboratory in Pietermaritzburg.

Her team’s results, now presented in a peer-reviewed research paper, showed she was right in her hunch that the fungus could be used in the fight against the armyworms.

It was a major breakthrough, said Mathulwe, because while there are chemical treatments for dealing with the caterpillars in the early stages of life, nothing has proven effective against mature populations.

The African armyworm not only eats staple crops such as maize and sorghum but also releases a chemical compound in grass that can make cattle sick.

The impact can be brutal for farmers. One outbreak in 2017 was estimated to have destroyed up to 40% of Zambia’s maize production.

It also sends food prices soaring and puts strain on government budgets. Last year’s outbreak caused problems for farmers in countries such as Zimbabwe, where inflation had hit 736% in 2024, and Malawi, where it reached 35% in 2024.

The African armyworm causes the most damage in its caterpillar stage but is also hard to control when it develops into a moth, allowing populations to migrate.

“When we discovered this fungus, we realised we could develop this into a product that can be eventually used when the next outbreak happens,” said Mathulwe.

“I think it will be a great thing – it will eventually eliminate the fear for farmers that the insect creates because once it’s present within grazing fields, farmers start to panic.”

Mathulwe said there was still more work and more testing to do in developing a product for use by farmers.

“I think it will create a lot of hope for farmers, because it will mean that their animals won’t get sick if the farmer is able to control the presence of the insects within their field,” she said.

world.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
world.snippet: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta Spain has announced it will introduce tempora...
world.content:
Spain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.

The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.

Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.

The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.

The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.

The Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.

Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.

“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.

He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.

Meloni’s office said in a statement: “Italy does not accept ultimatums or impositions from abroad regarding national security and border control.

“Only when there is certainty that there are no security or terrorism risks to Italy, that no new wave is occurring, and that no irregular migrants are heading toward European territory, will the decision be reconsidered.”

Spain’s interior ministry announced the reciprocal measures within hours.

Spanish police have been monitoring online rumours and social media about possible fresh arrivals in Ceuta in mid-August, according to local media. But authorities have not expressly said they expect a repeat of last week’s rush.

Border authorities would in the meantime “do their utmost to ensure maximum ease of movement for Spanish and European citizens” who are not affected by border checks, the Italian statement added.

Italy, which does not share a land border with Spain, introduced border controls at maritime and air entry points for third-country nationals arriving from Spain.

The move, announced on 31 July, was an “extraordinary measure” intended to “safeguard national security and prevent possible repercussions for our nation”, Meloni said at the time.

She was among several EU leaders who called for Spain to be suspended from the visa-free Schengen travel zone after the Ceuta incident, despite such a move being legally impossible.

Italy’s coalition government has sought to stop the tens of thousands of people who land in small boats on the country’s shores each year.

The Spanish government warned against “creating rifts and sterile conflicts driven by internal electoral motives” and said “we trust that pro-European sentiment, common sense and good faith prevail”.

Of the 72,000 people who entered Ceuta, 70,000 have returned to Morocco, according to official Spanish figures.

Spanish authorities said 80 people died in the crossings.

Moroccan rights groups, however, estimate the figure to be higher. The Moroccan Association for Human Rights and the European Coordination for Human Rights in Morocco on Friday said at least 141 deaths were recorded and that the toll was likely to rise.

Morocco’s interior ministry has said 11 people died on its side of the border, all but one by drowning.

Those who remain in Ceuta – including hundreds of unaccompanied children – face dire living conditions with little access to food, water and shelter.

world.title: Judge approves Trump effort to end South Sudan TPS protections
world.snippet: Decision follows supreme court ruling that allowed US government to strip protections for Haitians and Syrians Temporary protected status...
world.content:
Temporary protected status (TPS) for hundreds of South Sudanese nationals in the United States is set to end after a federal judge ruled that the Trump administration can move forward with stripping their protections.

On Friday, US district judge Patti Saris of the district of Massachusetts rejected an attempt by immigrant rights organizations including the New York-based African Communities Together to keep TPS for South Sudanese nationals living in the US.

Saris’s decision follows a 6-3 supreme court ruling in June allowing the Trump administration to strip hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians of TPS, which granted them permission to work and live legally in the US.

The supreme court’s conservative majority overturned lower court rulings in New York and Washington DC, which had blocked the administration from ending TPS for more than 350,000 Haitians and about 6,100 Syrians.

A TPS designation allows eligible people from certain countries facing crises including civil war and environmental disasters to remain in the US temporarily, protects them from deportation and allows them to work legally.

In her 15-page ruling, Saris wrote that “as a logical matter, plaintiffs’ arguments rest upon a self-contradictory, self-defeating foundation”.

According to Saris, the plaintiffs’ argument undermined itself, because if the homeland security department (DHS) lacked the authority to terminate South Sudan’s TPS designation, it also would have lacked the authority to issue the designation initially.

“South Sudan’s original TPS designation would thus be invalid by the same token as its termination,” Saris wrote.

In response to the ruling, James Percival, a DHS general counsel said on X: “Every other TPS judge must do the same! Every day these ‘administrative stays’ are in effect is a day the American people are denied what they voted for.”

The Guardian has contacted African Communities Together for comment.

Meanwhile, in a statement on Friday, the immigrant advocacy organization Global Refuge condemned the ruling. The CEO, Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, said: “The reality of the situation is that South Sudan is on the brink of a return to an all-out-civil war. Roughly two-thirds of the population, some 10 million people, now depend on humanitarian aid to survive.

“With only several hundred South Sudanese holding TPS in the US right now, this isn’t a policy forced by scale or strain on our system. To the contrary, this is the administration’s deliberate choice to send a small group of vulnerable individuals and families back into a country where civilians are bearing the brunt of intensifying violence and displacement,” Vignarajah added.

The Trump administration’s effort to strip TPS protections from hundreds of thousands of immigrants comes despite the US government’s own highest-level travel warnings for Americans to several countries affected, including South Sudan, Haiti and Syria.

In the case of South Sudan, the country has been ravaged by years of civil war and political instability that have displaced millions. Since gaining independence in 2011, more than 400,000 people have been killed in conflict, with fighting and ethnic violence continuing to claim civilian lives.

The DHS moved in November to terminate TPS for South Sudan, saying the country ‌no longer met the conditions for the designation, which was first issued in 2011. The department’s action would have led to the end of protections for more than 232 South Sudanese and at least 73 South Sudanese with pending applications. An earlier order by Saris had blocked that from happening.

After the supreme court’s ruling, lawyers for a group of South Sudanese nationals and the non-profit African Communities Together urged Saris to once again block the ‌end of TPS on new grounds that the justices had not addressed.

That included an argument that the DHS lacked authority to terminate TPS because the statute that created the TPS program in 1990 referred ​only to the attorney general as the official who had authority to extend and terminate the deportation protections.

The DHS was established later, in 2002, after the September 11 attacks.

Most of the justice department’s immigration-related functions were transferred to it at that time. Saris, who was appointed by Bill Clinton, concluded Congress had likewise transferred authority over TPS to the DHS.

Since 2001, TPS holders have paid $7.8bn annually in taxes and contributed $262bn to the US economy, according to the advocacy organization Fwd.us. Many TPS holders are employed in critical industries already facing worker shortages across the country, including construction, hospitality and healthcare.

Losing TPS can leave immigrants without legal status vulnerable to arrest, detention and deportation, even with pending asylum or green card applications.

Some may face immigration court proceedings with limited options to stay in the US. People ordered removed could be deported and barred from returning for years.

Reuters contributed reporting
